title: What is the role of `finalize()` in garbage collection, and why is it deprecated?
shortTitle: What is finalize() and why is it deprecated?

s1_definition.profdef: `finalize()` is a method inherited from `Object` that the garbage collector was intended to call on an object just before reclaiming it, giving the object a last chance to release resources. In practice it is unreliable and dangerous: there is no guarantee it ever runs, no guarantee of timing, it adds collection overhead, it can resurrect objects, and exceptions inside it are swallowed. For these reasons it has been deprecated since Java 9 and marked for removal, and the recommended replacements are try-with-resources with `AutoCloseable` and, for post-mortem cleanup, the `java.lang.ref.Cleaner` API.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India left a note on each storage box saying "before you throw me away, please also shred the papers inside." The problem is the cleanup crew is not required to read the note, might read it much later, might never get to it before the building closes for the day, and if the note's instructions fail, nobody is told. Relying on that note to shred sensitive documents would be reckless. Instead the bank adopts a strict rule that whoever opens a file must close and shred it themselves when done, which is exactly what try-with-resources enforces.
s1_definition.oneliner: finalize() was a last-chance cleanup hook, but it is unreliable, slow, and unsafe, so it is deprecated in favor of try-with-resources and the Cleaner API.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `finalize()` is a method inherited from `Object` that the garbage collector was intended to call on an object just before reclaiming it, giving the object a last chance to release resources. In practice it is unreliable and dangerous: there is no guarantee it ever runs, no guarantee of timing, it adds collection overhead, it can resurrect objects, and exceptions inside it are swallowed. For these reasons it has been deprecated since Java 9 and marked for removal, and the recommended replacements are try-with-resources with `AutoCloseable` and, for post-mortem cleanup, the `java.lang.ref.Cleaner` API.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India left a note on each storage box saying "before you throw me away, please also shred the papers inside." The problem is the cleanup crew is not required to read the note, might read it much later, might never get to it before the building closes for the day, and if the note's instructions fail, nobody is told. Relying on that note to shred sensitive documents would be reckless. Instead the bank adopts a strict rule that whoever opens a file must close and shred it themselves when done, which is exactly what try-with-resources enforces.

**One line to remember:** finalize() was a last-chance cleanup hook, but it is unreliable, slow, and unsafe, so it is deprecated in favor of try-with-resources and the Cleaner API.

sections.s2_technical:
The original intent of finalize was to let an object clean up native or external resources right before the collector reclaimed it, similar to a destructor in C++. You would override `protected void finalize()` and close a file handle or free a native buffer there. In theory this gave a safety net if the programmer forgot to release something.

The problems are severe and well documented. First, there is no guarantee finalize will ever be called; if the program exits before the object is collected, it never runs, so you cannot rely on it to release critical resources. Second, there is no guarantee of when it runs; the object may sit for a long time before the collector gets to it, so a file handle could stay open far longer than expected, exhausting handles under load. Third, it hurts performance, because objects with a finalizer require an extra collection cycle: they are placed on a finalization queue, processed by a separate finalizer thread, and only collected on a later pass, which can double the time to reclaim them.

There are even correctness hazards. Inside finalize you can accidentally store `this` into a static field, resurrecting the object so it is no longer garbage, which breaks the collector's assumptions. Any exception thrown inside finalize is ignored and the finalization of that object simply stops, so errors vanish silently. And finalizers can create security and ordering issues, which is why they are considered an anti-pattern.

The correct modern approaches are clear. For resources with a clear scope, implement `AutoCloseable` and use try-with-resources, so cleanup is deterministic and happens exactly when the block ends, even on exception. For example `try (var session = openLedgerSession()) { ... }` guarantees close runs. For the rare case where you need a safety net tied to unreachability, use the `Cleaner` API, where you register a cleaning action that runs when the object becomes phantom-reachable, without the pitfalls of finalize. A senior nuance is that even Cleaner should be a backstop, not the primary strategy, because its timing is still non-deterministic; the primary strategy should always be explicit, scoped closing.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India had a class that opened a connection to a ledger system and relied on finalize to close it. Under heavy load during month-end, connections piled up because finalize ran too late, and the service ran out of connections and started rejecting transfers. This is exactly why finalize is unsafe for resource release, because its timing is not guaranteed and critical resources leaked under pressure.

Problem 2 — The fix was to make the ledger session implement AutoCloseable and use try-with-resources, so the connection closes deterministically the moment the work block ends. This is exactly the recommended replacement, and showing the broken finalize approach beside the correct AutoCloseable approach makes the lesson concrete.

In the mini-project we contrast both. We define an `Account`, a broken `LegacyLedgerSession` that overrides finalize, and a correct `LedgerSession` that implements AutoCloseable. The demo performs a transfer between Rajesh and Priya using the AutoCloseable session inside try-with-resources, showing deterministic close, and explains why the finalize version is unreliable. We log open and close events to make timing visible.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh (SAV2001, 1000000) and Priya (CUR3001, 250000), a transfer of 50000 inside an AutoCloseable session, and a legacy finalize-based session.

Step 1: The try-with-resources statement creates a LedgerSession, whose constructor logs that the session is OPEN and conceptually acquires a ledger connection. The session reference is scoped to the try block.

Step 2: Inside the block, session.transfer runs, debiting Rajesh to 950000 and crediting Priya to 300000, and logs the transfer within the named session.

Step 3: The try block ends, so the JVM automatically calls close on the session. This runs deterministically at this exact point, logging that the session is CLOSED, which guarantees the connection is released immediately, even if the transfer had thrown an exception.

Step 4: The demo then creates a LegacyLedgerSession and sets its reference to null. Dropping the reference only makes the object eligible for collection; it does not promptly run finalize. The connection it holds may stay open for an unknown time, or finalize may never run if the program exits first, which is the core danger.

Step 5: The demo logs a warning that the legacy approach's cleanup timing is not guaranteed. Whether the finalize message prints at all is up to the collector, which visibly demonstrates its unreliability compared to the deterministic close.

```text
[INFO] Ledger session OPEN: month-end
[INFO] Transferred Rs.50000 within session month-end
[INFO] Ledger session CLOSED deterministically: month-end
[INFO] Rajesh Rs.950000, Priya Rs.300000
[INFO] Legacy session OPEN: legacy
[WARNING] LegacyLedgerSession relies on finalize → close timing NOT guaranteed
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  CORRECT PATH (AutoCloseable + try-with-resources)
    open session ──▶ transfer ──▶ block ends ──▶ close() GUARANTEED here
    (resource released deterministically, even on exception)

  ANTI-PATTERN PATH (finalize)
    open legacy ──▶ ref = null ──▶ object eligible for GC
                                      │ maybe later / maybe never
                                      ▼
                               finalize() runs?  NOT GUARANTEED
    (resource may leak under load → connection exhaustion)
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```text

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Payment Service                              │
  │   try (LedgerSession s = pool.borrow()) {      │
  │      s.transfer(...)                           │

  └───────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — finalize vs modern cleanup ═══

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │   <<interface>> AutoCloseable │
  │  + close()                   │  called by try-with-resources
  └──────────────┬───────────────┘
      implements  │
                  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │        LedgerSession          │
  │  + close(): deterministic     │
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  finalize() problems:
    - no guarantee it runs            → resource may leak forever
    - no timing guarantee             → late release, handle exhaustion
    - extra GC cycle (finalizer queue)→ slower reclamation
    - can resurrect 'this'            → breaks collector assumptions
    - swallows exceptions             → silent failures
  Replacements:
    AutoCloseable + try-with-resources  (primary, deterministic)
    java.lang.ref.Cleaner               (backstop, phantom-reachable)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The finalize method is a method inherited from Object that the garbage collector was originally intended to call on an object just before reclaiming it, so the object could release native or external resources as a last chance, similar to a destructor in C++. The idea was a safety net if a programmer forgot to free something, and you implemented it by overriding finalize to close a handle or free a buffer.

The reason it is deprecated since Java 9 and marked for removal is that it is unreliable and dangerous on several fronts. There is no guarantee it ever runs, because if the program exits before the object is collected, finalize never executes, so you cannot depend on it for critical cleanup. There is no guarantee of timing either, so a resource like a database connection could stay open far longer than expected, which under load leads to handle or connection exhaustion. It also hurts performance, because an object with a finalizer needs an extra collection cycle, going onto a finalization queue and being processed by a separate thread before it can actually be reclaimed.

On top of that there are correctness hazards. Inside finalize you can accidentally resurrect the object by storing a reference to it somewhere reachable, which breaks the collector's assumptions, and any exception thrown inside finalize is silently swallowed so failures disappear. All of this is why finalize is considered an anti-pattern. In my banking work we actually got burned by this: a ledger session relied on finalize to close its connection, and during month-end load the connections piled up because finalize ran too late, and the service started rejecting transfers.

The correct modern approach is deterministic cleanup. For resources with a clear scope I implement AutoCloseable and use try-with-resources, so close runs exactly when the block ends, even if an exception is thrown, which is what fixed our connection problem. For the rare case where I want a safety net tied to the object becoming unreachable, I use the Cleaner API, which runs a cleaning action when the object is phantom-reachable without the pitfalls of finalize. One senior nuance I always add is that even Cleaner should be a backstop and not the primary strategy, because its timing is still non-deterministic, so the primary strategy must always be explicit, scoped closing. So my complete answer is that finalize was a last-chance cleanup hook that is unreliable, slow, and unsafe, which is why it is deprecated, and I replace it with AutoCloseable and try-with-resources for deterministic release, falling back to Cleaner only as a safety net.

---

keyPoints: finalize(): called by GC before reclaiming an object — cleanup hook
Deprecated: unpredictable timing, may never run, delays GC, resurrects objects
Never rely on finalize() for critical resource cleanup
